Vignette:
# Kofi's Vigil

Kofi Mensah was fifty-five years old and had spent thirty-two of those years painting—first in Accra, then in Atlanta after his marriage to Diana, and for the last two decades in their modest home in Decatur, Georgia, where he'd built a steady reputation for meticulous restoration work on historic properties. He was a man of routine and precision, the kind who arrived at job sites with his brushes cleaned and organized, who took pride in the evenness of his strokes, who knew the names of his regular clients and remembered which of their children had gone to college. His life had the shape of something well-constructed.

On a Tuesday evening in March, his younger brother Kwesi had called from the hospital. Their father, Samuel, had collapsed at home that afternoon—a heart attack, massive and sudden. Kofi had driven to Grady Memorial with Diana gripping his forearm, and they arrived to find his mother in the waiting room, her hands shaking so violently she could not hold a cup of water. The doctor emerged within the hour to say that Samuel had not survived the ambulance ride. He was gone before they reached the hospital doors. Kofi remembered the specific moment the doctor said this—the fluorescent lights overhead, the smell of antiseptic, the sound of an ambulance siren wailing past outside, and the absolute incomprehensibility of the words. His father, who had called him three days earlier to ask about a painting project, who had made plans to visit in April, who had been alive that morning, was simply not anymore.

The weeks that followed were a blur of funeral arrangements, relatives arriving from Ghana, the rituals of mourning. But something had shifted in Kofi's nervous system in that hospital waiting room, something that did not shift back. Within days of the funeral, he noticed that his shoulders lived somewhere near his ears now. His jaw clenched without his awareness. At night, he would lie awake beside Diana, listening to the house settle around them, convinced that something catastrophic was about to happen—another collapse, another siren, another irrevocable loss. He had come to believe that safety was an illusion, that danger lived inside his own home, waiting. Even in daylight, when he was at a job site painting a Victorian's trim, his body remained coiled, muscles ready to spring. He was constantly scanning, constantly waiting for the next ambulance.

Within two months, he had stopped answering calls from his brother-in-law, who had lost his own mother that spring. When a neighbor mentioned her sister's passing at the grocery store, Kofi had felt his chest tighten so acutely that he'd excused himself and sat in his truck for twenty minutes, unable to breathe properly. Talk of death—anyone's death—had become unbearable. He began to avoid his regular clients' homes if he knew they were grieving. He turned down a major restoration job because the homeowner had recently lost her husband. Diana had asked him gently why he was declining work, and he could not quite explain it: that being near other people's losses felt like stepping into a trap, that their grief was somehow contagious, that if he let himself get close to anyone else's pain, his own might consume him entirely.

His sleep had become fragmented. He would wake at three in the morning, his body drenched in sweat, gripped by a sensation of impending doom that had no image attached to it—just the raw, overwhelming terror of loss itself, the certainty that someone he loved was slipping away right now, in the dark. When he tried to remember his father's face, sometimes nothing came except the feeling: the crushing weight of grief, the suffocation of it. Other times, he saw the hospital corridor with photographic clarity, saw the doctor's mouth moving, saw the moment his mother's hands began to shake.

Kofi had stopped going out in the evenings. He no longer attended his church. He had become someone he did not recognize—someone isolated, hypervigilant, someone who believed his life had been irrevocably destroyed by a single moment. Diana had finally insisted he see someone after she found him sitting in their driveway at two in the morning, unable to explain what he was doing there. He had come to therapy because his wife had asked him to, because he could no longer hide the fact that he was drowning, and because some small part of him—the part that still remembered being a man who built beautiful things—wondered if there might be any way back from this.
